opus-5.5.text:
I think "agent" is actually a very old concept. In reinforcement learning, which is the field I've worked in for many years, the agent was always there from the very beginning. The textbook definition is simple: an agent is something that lives in an environment, observes the state of that environment, takes actions, and receives feedback, and its goal is to accomplish some task or maximize some reward over time. So in that sense, an agent is not new at all.

What's new in the era of large language models is that, for the first time, we have agents that are general. Before, if you trained an RL agent to play Go or StarCraft or to control a robot arm, it could only do that one thing. You had to design the environment, the action space, and the reward very carefully, and the agent you got was very narrow. Now, with large language models, we have a kind of foundation that already understands language, has a lot of common sense and world knowledge, and can reason to some extent. So when people talk about agents today, I think what they really mean is taking this general-purpose brain and letting it actually act, letting it use tools, browse the web, write and run code, operate a computer, and interact with people, over multiple steps, to finish a task for you.

The way I usually put it is this: a chatbot answers your question, but an agent does the job for you. A chatbot is one round. You ask, it replies, and it's done. An agent has to plan, take an action, see what happens, adjust, and keep going, sometimes for dozens or hundreds of steps. That loop of interacting with an environment is the key difference, and it's also exactly where reinforcement learning comes back into the picture. Pretraining gives the model knowledge, but learning to act well over a long sequence of decisions, to recover from mistakes, and to know when a task is actually finished is something you really need RL and real interaction to learn.

So my understanding is that the LLM era turned "agent" from an academic concept into something that could be a real product. But I'd also say we're still quite early. Today's agents can do some impressive demos, but making them reliable on long, complex, real-world tasks is still a very hard problem, and that's what a lot of us are working on right now.

r001.rationale: It describes an agent as interacting with an environment over time, but does not explain the term as an extension of game theory to sequential decision problems.

r002.rationale: It defines an RL agent as something that lives in an environment, observes its state, takes actions, and receives feedback.

r003.rationale: It says LLM-era agents act through tools and external interfaces, including browsing the web, running code, operating a computer, and interacting with people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yi Wu: That's a good place to start, because the word gets used in so many ways now that people often end up talking past each other. Let me try to give my own working definition.

For me, an agent is a system that can perceive its environment, make decisions, take actions, and then observe the consequences of those actions and adjust. That closed loop is the key part. If you look at the classic reinforcement learning formulation, that's exactly what an agent is: there is an environment, there is a policy, the policy takes in observations and outputs actions, the environment gives back new observations and some reward signal, and the whole thing iterates. In that sense the concept is actually quite old. It predates large language models by decades.

What changed with LLMs is that the "brain" of the agent suddenly got a lot more general. Before, if you wanted an agent that could play Go, you trained a policy for Go. If you wanted one that could control a robot arm, you trained a separate policy for that. Each agent was narrow. The language model gives you a component that already carries a huge amount of world knowledge and can reason in natural language, so you can plug it into many different environments and it has at least some competence out of the box. That's why people got excited: the same base model can browse the web, write code, call tools, operate software. It feels like a step toward a general-purpose agent.

But I'd push back a little on how loosely the term gets applied today. A lot of what gets marketed as an "agent" is really a chatbot with a few API calls wrapped around it. If the model answers a question and the interaction ends, I wouldn't call that an agent. To me the distinguishing features are, first, that it has a goal that extends beyond a single turn; second, that it can take actions that actually change the state of the world, not just produce text for a human to read; and third, that it can observe the result and correct itself when things go wrong. That last part, the feedback and self-correction, is where most current systems are still weak.

There's also a difference between an agent in the research sense and an agent in the product sense. In research, I care about whether the system is actually learning from interaction, whether it gets better through trial and error in a given environment. In the product sense, people mostly mean autonomy: can I give it a task and walk away. Both are legitimate, but they lead to different technical priorities. The research direction cares about training signals, exploration, long-horizon credit assignment. The product direction cares about reliability, tool integration, and keeping the model from doing something stupid or dangerous when nobody is watching.

So if I had to compress it: an agent is a decision-maker embedded in a loop with an environment. The language model is a powerful new kind of decision-maker, but the loop is what makes it an agent. And I think the most interesting work right now is about closing that loop properly, letting these models learn from their own actions rather than just imitating text written by humans.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning agents as acting in an environment through a policy and feedback loop, but does not explain the term’s origin as an extension of game theory to sequential decision problems.

r002.rationale: It defines an agent as perceiving an environment, making decisions, taking actions, and observing their consequences; it also describes the RL agent-environment loop.

r003.rationale: It says LLM-based systems can browse the web, write code, call tools, and operate software, and notes that systems with API calls are often marketed as agents. Together these convey the common interface-calling sense.

astra-6.text:
I think “agent” is a broad concept. The key is that it doesn’t just produce an answer—it interacts with an environment in pursuit of a goal. It observes what is happening, decides what to do, takes an action, and then uses the result to decide its next step. That cycle is more fundamental than whether the system uses a large language model.

In the context of large language models, we can think of the model as one component of that cycle. It can interpret a task, make a plan, and choose tools. But an agent also needs some way to execute actions and receive feedback. If you ask a model how to organize a trip, it might give you advice. If you give a system your constraints and it searches for options, checks whether they fit, and revises its plan based on what it finds, that starts to look like an agent.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply at whether a system can call a tool. What matters is whether it can keep making progress toward a goal through interaction. And the difficult part is doing that reliably: recognizing mistakes, adjusting when circumstances change, and knowing when to ask a person for help.

r001.rationale: The response describes sequential interaction and decision-making, but does not explain the term’s connection to reinforcement learning or its extension of game theory.

r002.rationale: It defines an agent as interacting with an environment toward a goal, observing outcomes and acting in response.

r003.rationale: It mentions that a model can choose tools and that systems can call tools, but says tool calling alone does not define an agent; it does not state that LLM discourse often uses “agent” to mean a model’s ability to call external-world interfaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “agent” describes a way of using a model, rather than a particular kind of model. Instead of simply answering a question, the system pursues a goal: it observes what is happening, decides what to do, takes an action, and then uses the result to decide its next step.

For example, if you ask a model how to organize a trip, it can give you advice. An agent might look up options, compare them against your preferences, build an itinerary, and revise it when something changes. The key difference is that its actions affect the situation, and it has to respond to the consequences.

But I wouldn’t draw a sharp line between an assistant and an agent. There are degrees of autonomy. A system might handle a few steps independently and ask you before making a consequential decision. What matters is whether it can reliably carry a task forward over multiple steps—not just produce a convincing description of what it would do.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent as acting through sequential steps, but does not connect the term to reinforcement learning or its extension of game theory to sequential decision problems.

r002.rationale: It describes observing and acting on a situation, but does not define an agent in reinforcement learning as an AI that interacts with an environment.

r003.rationale: It says an agent’s actions affect the situation, but does not state that LLM discourse often uses “agent” for a model’s ability to call external-world interfaces.
